title: Midwifery infusions: oxytocin, magnesium sulfate and the 80 mL/h limit
blurb: Set pump rates for magnesium sulfate and oxytocin, and work within the 80 mL/hour fluid limit in severe pre-eclampsia.
question: A woman with severe pre-eclampsia is prescribed magnesium sulfate 1 g per hour from a bag of 20 g in 500 mL. At what rate should the pump be set?

teach.body: Formal rule: pump rate (mL/hour) = volume (mL) ÷ time (hours). For a dose-based infusion, rate = dose per hour ÷ concentration, where concentration = amount in the bag ÷ bag volume. Plain English: find how much drug is in each mL, then ask how many mL deliver one hour's dose. Every strength, bag and limit you need is printed in the stem.
teach.cite: FACTS.md section 4; NICE NG133 recs 1.8.4 and 1.8.12

teach.caption: NG133 allows more than 80 mL/hour when there are ongoing losses such as haemorrhage.

teach.h: Worked example: Amara on the labour ward
teach.body: Amara Okafor, 29, has severe pre-eclampsia. Prescription: magnesium sulfate 1 g/hour; the bag holds 10 g in 250 mL. Concentration = 10 ÷ 250 = 0.04 g/mL. Rate = 1 ÷ 0.04 = 25 mL/hour. Shortcut: 250 mL holds 10 g, so 1 g sits in 25 mL. Her loading dose, 4 g in 60 mL over 15 minutes, runs at 60 ÷ 0.25 h = 240 mL/hour. Sense-check: 60 mL in a quarter of an hour is 4 × 60 in a full hour.

NICE NG133 says to limit maintenance fluids to 80 mL/hour in severe pre-eclampsia unless there are ongoing losses. Some unit protocols go further and cap total intravenous fluids, every line included, at 80 mL/hour; a stem using that rule will say it is the unit protocol. Exam method: read which lines the stem says count, add their rates, subtract from 80. Example: magnesium at 25 mL/hour and labetalol at 20 mL/hour leave 80 − 25 − 20 = 35 mL/hour for maintenance fluid. At 80 mL/hour, the volume given over a shift = 80 × hours.

teach.h: Oxytocin: units per hour and mL per hour
teach.body: Oxytocin is measured in units (1 unit = 1000 milliunits). Example: 40 units in 500 mL gives 0.08 units/mL; running at 125 mL/hour the woman receives 125 × 0.08 = 10 units/hour. For a milliunits-per-minute prescription, convert twice: × 60 for hours, ÷ 1000 for units, then divide by the concentration. Third-stage doses (10 units IM, or 5 units slow IV) come from NICE NG235.

rows.label: 2 milliunits/min
values: Per minute used as per hour

teach.text: Minutes left as minutes: 60 mL over 15 minutes is 240 mL/hour, not 4 mL/hour (60 ÷ 15). Change minutes to hours first (15 minutes = 0.25 hours). And with the 80 mL/hour limit, subtract every line the stem says counts, not just the first one you see.

items: Concentration = amount in bag ÷ bag volume.
Minutes → hours before dividing; milliunits → units (÷ 1000).
NG133: magnesium 4 g loading, then 1 g/hour for 24 hours.
NG133: maintenance fluids limited to 80 mL/hour in severe pre-eclampsia.
Classic error: inverting the concentration or leaving time in minutes.

summary: You can now turn a magnesium sulfate or oxytocin prescription into a pump rate in mL per hour, and convert minutes and milliunits correctly. You can also apply a unit protocol's 80 mL/hour total-fluid limit by subtracting every running line.

A.q: A woman with severe pre-eclampsia is prescribed magnesium sulfate 1 g per hour by intravenous infusion. The bag contains magnesium sulfate 20 g in 400 mL. At what rate should the infusion pump be set?
A.why: Concentration = 20 g ÷ 400 mL = 0.05 g/mL. Rate = 1 g/hour ÷ 0.05 g/mL = 20 mL/hour. Check: 400 mL holds 20 g, so 1 g is in 20 mL.

whyNot.0: Inverted the concentration (g per mL) instead of finding the mL that hold 1 g.
whyNot.2: Ran the whole bag in one hour.
whyNot.3: Divided the bag by the 24-hour treatment length; the bag lasts 20 hours at 1 g/hour.

A.q: A woman is prescribed a loading dose of magnesium sulfate 4 g diluted to 40 mL, intravenously over 10 minutes. At what rate should the infusion pump be set?
A.why: 10 minutes = 10 ÷ 60 hours. Rate = 40 ÷ (10 ÷ 60) = 40 × 6 = 240 mL/hour. Sense-check: 40 mL every 10 minutes is 6 × 40 in an hour.

whyNot.0: Divided by 10 minutes as if it were 10 hours.
whyNot.1: Wrote 10 minutes as 0.1 hours; 10 minutes is 1/6 of an hour.
whyNot.2: Gave the volume as the rate; 40 mL in 10 minutes is far faster than 40 mL/hour.

A.q: An infusion of oxytocin 30 units in 500 mL 0.9% sodium chloride is running at 50 mL per hour. How many units of oxytocin is the woman receiving each hour?
A.why: Concentration = 30 ÷ 500 = 0.06 units/mL. Units per hour = 50 mL × 0.06 = 3 units.

whyNot.1: This is the concentration in each mL, not the hourly dose.
whyNot.3: Used a 1000 mL bag; the bag is 500 mL.

B.q: A woman with severe pre-eclampsia has magnesium sulfate running at 20 mL per hour. The unit protocol limits her total intravenous fluids to 80 mL per hour. What is the highest rate at which her maintenance fluid can run?
B.why: Limit 80 mL/hour − magnesium 20 mL/hour = 60 mL/hour for maintenance fluid.

whyNot.0: Forgot to subtract the magnesium line, which counts within the limit.
whyNot.1: Added the magnesium rate to the limit instead of subtracting it.

B.q: A woman with severe pre-eclampsia receives intravenous fluids at 80 mL per hour for 9 hours. What total volume does she receive? Please use the correct unit.
B.why: Volume = rate × time = 80 mL/hour × 9 hours = 720 mL.

whyNot.1: Added the rate and the hours instead of multiplying.
whyNot.2: Divided the rate by the hours; that gives no meaningful volume.

B.q: A woman receives a magnesium sulfate loading dose of 4 g, then an infusion of 1 g per hour from 1400 until it is stopped at 0800 the next day. What total dose of magnesium sulfate does she receive? Please use the correct unit.
B.why: 1400 to 0800 = 18 hours, so infusion = 18 × 1 g = 18 g. Total = 4 g + 18 g = 22 g.

whyNot.0: Counted the infusion but left out the 4 g loading dose.
whyNot.1: Assumed 24 hours of infusion; 1400 to 0800 is 18 hours.
whyNot.2: Counted 19 hours by including both end points; the infusion ran 18 hours.

C.q: A woman in labour is prescribed oxytocin at 4 milliunits per minute. The infusion contains oxytocin 10 units in 500 mL. At what rate should the infusion pump be set?
C.why: Dose per hour = 4 milliunits × 60 = 240 milliunits = 0.24 units. Concentration = 10 ÷ 500 = 0.02 units/mL. Rate = 0.24 ÷ 0.02 = 12 mL/hour.

whyNot.0: Worked out mL per minute (0.2) and did not multiply by 60.
whyNot.2: Used milliunits as if they were units (missed ÷ 1000).

C.q: A woman with severe pre-eclampsia is prescribed magnesium sulfate 1 g per hour from a bag of 20 g in 500 mL, and labetalol is running at 16 mL per hour. The unit protocol limits her total intravenous fluids to 80 mL per hour. What is the highest rate for any other intravenous fluid?

whyNot.1: Subtracted the magnesium rate but forgot the labetalol line.
whyNot.2: Subtracted labetalol but not the magnesium rate (25 mL/hour).
whyNot.3: Added the running lines to the limit instead of subtracting.

C.q: A woman with postpartum haemorrhage is prescribed oxytocin 7.5 units per hour. The infusion contains oxytocin 40 units in 500 mL. At what rate should the infusion pump be set? Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
C.why: Concentration = 40 ÷ 500 = 0.08 units/mL. Rate = 7.5 ÷ 0.08 = 93.75, so 94 mL/hour to the nearest whole number.

whyNot.0: Multiplied by the concentration instead of dividing (units × units/mL).
whyNot.3: Divided the bag volume by the dose, missing the 40 units in the bag.

reteach.title: Concentration first, then divide
reteach.question: Magnesium sulfate 1 g/hour from a bag of 20 g in 500 mL: what rate?

blocks.body: 500 mL holds 20 g, so each gram sits in 500 ÷ 20 = 25 mL. One gram per hour therefore needs 25 mL per hour. The same logic works for oxytocin units: mL per unit, times units per hour.

blocks.text: Dividing the other way round (20 ÷ 500 = 0.04) gives grams per mL, not a pump rate. A pump rate of 0.04 mL/hour would deliver almost nothing.

explain.body: Concentration = amount in the bag ÷ bag volume. It tells you how much drug is in 1 mL.

test.q: A bag contains magnesium sulfate 20 g in 500 mL. How much magnesium sulfate is in each mL?
test.why: 20 g ÷ 500 mL = 0.04 g in each mL.

whyNot.0: Inverted: 25 is mL per gram, not grams per mL.
whyNot.3: Decimal slip: one place too far (0.004).

test.q: A volume of 30 mL is to be given by pump over 15 minutes. At what rate should the pump be set?

whyNot.0: Divided by 15 as if the time were in hours.
whyNot.2: Multiplied the volume by the minutes.
whyNot.3: Wrote 15 minutes as 0.15 hours; it is 0.25 hours.

explain.body: NICE NG133 limits maintenance fluids to 80 mL/hour. When the stem says a unit protocol limits total IV fluids to 80 mL/hour, subtract every running line from 80 to find what is left.
explain.cite: NICE NG133 rec 1.8.12 (maintenance fluids); total-fluid caps are unit protocol

test.q: A woman with severe pre-eclampsia has one infusion running at 18 mL per hour. Her protocol limits total intravenous fluids to 80 mL per hour. What is the highest rate for her maintenance fluid?

whyNot.0: Did not subtract the running infusion.
whyNot.1: Added the running infusion to the limit.

explain.body: Units per hour = mL per hour × concentration (units per mL).

test.q: An infusion of oxytocin 40 units in 500 mL is running at 60 mL per hour. How many units of oxytocin is the woman receiving each hour? Write your answer to one decimal place.
test.why: Concentration = 40 ÷ 500 = 0.08 units/mL. Units per hour = 60 × 0.08 = 4.8 units.

whyNot.1: This is the concentration per mL, not the hourly dose.
whyNot.2: Used a 1000 mL bag (40 ÷ 1000 × 60); the bag is 500 mL.
